19999: Romans 16:7: was Junia a woman, and was she 'well known among the apostles' (an apostle herself) or 'well known to the apostles' (respected by them)? Most scholars now accept she was a woman, as John Chrysostom assumed when he praised her. The second question is still argued; Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace (2001) argued for 'to the apostles', and others, including Epp, have replied.
20000: What happened to the apostles: Bible and tradition
20001:
The Bible records very little. James son of Zebedee was killed with the sword by Herod Agrippa I around AD 44, the first of the Twelve to die. Judas Iscariot died after the betrayal; Matthew says he hanged himself and Acts says he fell headlong and burst open, two accounts that have been harmonised in different ways. Jesus foretold that Peter would be led where he did not want to go, 'to show by what kind of death he was to glorify God'. Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, and 2 Timothy has him expecting death.

Outside the Bible, three deaths are well attested. Peter and Paul died in Rome under Nero in the mid-60s (1 Clement, about AD 96, refers to their witness and suffering; later writers add that Peter was crucified and Paul beheaded). James the Lord's brother was stoned in Jerusalem in AD 62, according to the Jewish historian Josephus.

For most of the others we depend on later tradition of mixed quality. Early writers say John lived to old age in Ephesus. Thomas is linked with Parthia and India, Andrew with Scythia and Greece, Philip with Hierapolis, Bartholomew with India and Armenia. Stories of how each died, such as Andrew's X-shaped cross or Bartholomew being flayed, come mostly from apocryphal Acts written from the late second century onward, or from much later martyr lists.
20002: Myth: 'Every apostle except John died a martyr, and we know how.' The Bible records only James's martyrdom (and Judas's death). Peter, Paul and James the Lord's brother are well attested. For most others, the martyrdom stories are late and sometimes contradictory, and Clement of Alexandria preserves a second-century source (Heracleon) saying Matthew, Philip and Thomas did not die as martyrs. Sean McDowell's careful study rates each apostle's case separately.

20331: Jobs and Ministries in the Bible
20332: What did people in the Bible do for a living, what were the religious offices and ministries, and how did Jesus and Paul use ordinary work to teach about God?
20333: Most people in the Bible's world farmed, kept animals or worked a craft, usually in family businesses passed from parent to child. Some jobs carried honour (priest, scribe, landowner), others were looked down on (tanner, tax collector, shepherd in some periods), and many people were servants or slaves. Alongside daily work, Israel had sacred roles such as priest, Levite, prophet, judge and king, and the early church developed its own ministries: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, elders and deacons. Jesus and Paul drew constantly on ordinary work for their teaching: shepherds, sowers, fishermen, builders, soldiers, stewards and slaves all became pictures of life with God.
20334: Work is presented as good from the start: Adam is put in the garden 'to work it and keep it' before the fall.
20335: Most biblical work was agricultural or craft-based and family-run; trades were often inherited.
20336: Social status of a job varied: tax collectors were despised, tanners avoided, while scribes and priests were honoured.
20337: Israel's sacred offices (priest, Levite, prophet, judge, king, Nazirite) each had distinct rules and limits.
20338: The New Testament ministries of Ephesians 4:11 and the elders and deacons of the Pastoral Letters are interpreted differently across churches.
20339: Paul worked a trade to support himself while insisting ministers had a right to be paid.
20340: Many of Jesus' best-known parables come straight from the workplace.
20342:
Before sin enters the story, God places the first human in the garden 'to work it and keep it'. Work is part of being human, not a punishment. After the fall it becomes hard and frustrating: thorns, sweat and toil. The Bible keeps both sides in view.

Ancient Israel was a farming society. Families held land as an inheritance from God, and the law protected it from being permanently sold. Most households grew grain, olives and grapes, and kept sheep and goats. Craft skills such as pottery, weaving and metalwork were usually learned at home and passed down; Chronicles mentions families or guilds of linen workers and potters.

Proverbs praises hard work and warns against laziness. The 'excellent wife' of Proverbs 31 runs a household business: she buys a field, plants a vineyard, makes and sells cloth. The Sabbath command limited work for everyone, including servants, foreigners and animals.
20343: Land, animals and water: shepherds, farmers and fishermen
20344:
Shepherds appear everywhere in the Bible: Abel, the patriarchs, Rachel, Moses, David and Amos all kept flocks. A shepherd found pasture and water, protected the flock from lions, bears and thieves, and often slept beside the sheepfold. In Egypt shepherds were despised, and some later rabbinic texts treat herdsmen as unreliable witnesses, but in Israel's own story the shepherd is a picture of the ideal king and of God himself.

Farmers ploughed with oxen, sowed by hand, harvested with sickles and threshed on open floors. Gleaning laws let the poor gather what was left at the edges of fields. Vinedressers pruned and tended vineyards. Hunters such as Esau and Nimrod are mentioned but hunting was not a major livelihood.

On the Sea of Galilee, fishing was a significant business. Peter and Andrew, and James and John with their father Zebedee, worked with nets from boats and employed hired men. Fish were salted and traded, and a first-century boat found near Magdala in 1986 shows the kind of vessel they used.
20345: Myth: 'The disciples were poor, uneducated fishermen.' Zebedee's business had hired servants (Mark 1:20), and fishing families could be modestly prosperous. Acts calls Peter and John 'uneducated' (Acts 4:13), but the word means they lacked formal rabbinic training, not that they were illiterate peasants.
20347:
Jesus is called 'the tekton', usually translated 'carpenter'. The Greek word covers builders and craftsmen in wood and stone. Justin Martyr, writing in the second century, says Jesus made ploughs and yokes. Joseph had the same trade, and Nazareth was close to the building site of Sepphoris, rebuilt by Herod Antipas during Jesus' youth.

Paul, Priscilla and Aquila were 'tentmakers' (skenopoioi), which probably means they worked leather or cloth to make tents and awnings. Jeremiah watched a potter shape and reshape a vessel on his wheel. Bezalel and Oholiab were master craftsmen filled with God's Spirit to build the tabernacle. Lydia traded in purple cloth, a luxury dye. Dorcas made garments for widows. Simon of Joppa was a tanner, an occupation considered unclean by many because it handled dead animals; Peter stayed with him anyway.

Metalworkers forged tools and weapons; under the Philistines Israel had no smith of its own and had to go to Philistine smiths even to sharpen a ploughshare. Perfumers mixed spices and oils for anointing and burial.
20348: Myth: 'Jesus was a woodworker making furniture.' Tekton is broader: a builder or craftsman who might work in wood, stone or both. 'Carpenter' is not wrong, but the image of a fine furniture-maker is a later picture.
20350:
Merchants traded along caravan routes and by sea. Solomon's fleet and trade in horses and chariots made him rich, and the queen of Sheba arrived with a caravan of spices and gold. In the New Testament, Lydia was a businesswoman from Thyatira. Moneychangers in the temple court exchanged foreign coins for the Tyrian shekel used for the temple tax.

Tax collectors were among the most despised people in Jesus' world. Rome farmed out the right to collect tolls and taxes; collectors paid in advance and kept whatever extra they could extract. Jews who did this work, like Matthew and Zacchaeus, were seen as collaborators and cheats. The Gospels repeatedly pair 'tax collectors and sinners'.

Innkeepers ran lodging places, which had a poor reputation. Sailors worked the Mediterranean; Jonah's ship's crew and the crew on Paul's voyage to Rome give vivid pictures of ancient seamanship.
20351: Rahab is called a zonah (prostitute) in Joshua 2:1, and the New Testament keeps that description (Hebrews 11:31, James 2:25). The Aramaic Targum and Josephus (*Antiquities* 5.1.2) describe her instead as an innkeeper, possibly to soften the story. Most scholars take 'prostitute' as the plain meaning, while noting that inns and prostitution often overlapped.
20353:
Many people in the Bible were servants or slaves. Hebrew law allowed debt-servitude for Israelites with release in the seventh year, and Israel was told to remember that it had been a slave in Egypt. In the Roman world, slaves made up a large part of the population and could be labourers, household staff, teachers or business managers. Onesimus was a runaway slave whom Paul sent back to Philemon with a request to receive him 'as a beloved brother'. How these texts relate to slavery as an institution is discussed in detail elsewhere in the app.

Stewards managed a master's household and property: Joseph in Potiphar's house and later over all Egypt, and the stewards of Jesus' parables. Cupbearers, such as Nehemiah, tasted the king's wine and were trusted advisers. Scribes were trained in writing and law; Baruch wrote down Jeremiah's words and Ezra was 'a scribe skilled in the law of Moses'.

Soldiers appear from Joshua's army to the Roman centurions of the Gospels and Acts, several of whom are presented positively. Midwives Shiphrah and Puah defied Pharaoh. Luke is called 'the beloved physician'. Musicians served at court and in the temple.
20355:
Priests, all descended from Aaron, offered sacrifices, taught the law, judged cases of ritual purity and blessed the people. The high priest alone entered the Most Holy Place, once a year. Levites, members of the wider tribe of Levi, carried and guarded the tabernacle, later served as temple gatekeepers, musicians and teachers, and received tithes instead of land.

Prophets spoke God's word and could come from any background: Amos was a farmer, Jeremiah and Ezekiel were priests, Deborah was also a judge. Judges in the book of Judges were mainly deliverers raised up in crises; Deborah and Samuel also settled disputes. Kings were anointed and were meant to rule under God's law, writing out a copy for themselves.

The Nazirite vow was open to any man or woman: no wine, no haircut, no contact with the dead, for a set time. Samson and Samuel were Nazirites from birth, and Paul joined others in completing such a vow. Elders, senior men of a town or tribe, sat at the city gate to give judgments.
20357:
Paul says the risen Christ gave 'the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers' to equip the church. Apostles were sent witnesses who planted churches. Prophets spoke words from God for the church's encouragement and direction. Evangelists such as Philip announced the gospel. 'Shepherds and teachers', or pastors, cared for and taught local congregations.

The local leaders in Acts and the Pastoral Letters are elders (presbyteroi) and overseers (episkopoi); most scholars think these two words describe the same group in the New Testament period. Their qualifications are mostly character: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, able to teach. Deacons (diakonoi, 'servants') served alongside them; the seven chosen in Acts 6 to oversee food distribution are often seen as the first deacons. Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchreae. The church also kept a list of widows supported by the congregation who devoted themselves to prayer.

By the early second century, Ignatius of Antioch describes a single bishop over elders and deacons in each city. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches see this threefold ministry as a legitimate and lasting development; many Protestant churches see it as a later change from a plural eldership.
20358: Are all five ministries of Ephesians 4:11 meant to continue as offices today? Many Pentecostal and charismatic churches say yes; most other churches hold that apostles and prophets in the foundational sense ended with the first generation (Ephesians 2:20). Churches also disagree on whether Phoebe held a recognised office of deacon and whether women may serve as elders. See /debates/gender-roles and /movements/prophetic-movement.
20359: Should ministers be paid? Paul the tentmaker
20360:
Paul argues at length that those who preach the gospel have a right to be supported, quoting the law about not muzzling an ox and Jesus' own command. Elders who rule well, he says, are worthy of 'double honour'.

Yet Paul himself often refused support. He worked night and day with his hands so as not to be a burden, and so that no one could accuse him of preaching for money. In Corinth he worked alongside Priscilla and Aquila. He did accept gifts from the Philippians.

This fits Jewish practice of the time. A saying in the Mishnah commends combining study of the Torah with a worldly occupation, and many rabbis had trades. Greek and Roman elites, by contrast, often looked down on manual labour; Cicero lists wage-earning and craft work among the less respectable ways to make a living. Paul's choice to work with his hands would have struck some Greeks as undignified.
20361: Work as a picture: how Jesus and Paul used jobs
20362:
Jesus' parables come straight from the working world. A sower scatters seed on different soils. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one. A woman sweeps the house for a lost coin. Vineyard owners hire labourers at different hours and pay them the same. A merchant sells everything for one pearl. Stewards are trusted with money and called to account. He calls fishermen to 'fish for people' and calls himself the good shepherd, the true vine and a physician for the sick.

Paul uses work images just as freely. He calls himself a slave of Christ and a steward of God's mysteries. He planted and Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. He laid a foundation as a skilled master builder. He tells Timothy to be like a soldier, an athlete and a hard-working farmer. God is like a potter with clay. Jesus is the 'cornerstone' of a building of living stones.

These images assume the dignity of ordinary work. They also turn status upside down: the despised shepherd and the slave become pictures of Christ himself.
